title: Heights and Distances
summary: Applied trigonometry: angles of elevation and depression, the 30-45-60 rules, two-angle configurations, moving observers and compound figures. Every question reduces to one right triangle and one tangent — learn the three standard-angle multipliers and the cot-difference formula and this becomes near-guaranteed marks.

subtopics.title: Angles of elevation and depression
subtopics.concept:
The observer's eye is the origin; the **horizontal line** through the eye is the reference.

- **Elevation**: object is *above* eye level — the angle from the horizontal *up* to the line of sight.
- **Depression**: object is *below* eye level — the angle from the horizontal *down* to the line of sight.

Height raised on a platform: always work with the **eye level**, not the ground. The ground distance $d$ and the
height *above eye level* $h$ satisfy $\tan\theta=\dfrac{h}{d}$.

formulas.name: Depression = elevation
formulas.tex: \text{angle of depression at observer}=\text{angle of elevation at object}

tricks.title: Draw the horizontal through the eye
tricks.body:
One sketch kills most errors: horizontal dashed line from the eye, the line of sight, and the right angle
between them. Drop heights *below the eye* when the observer is elevated.

example.q: From a cliff top, a boat is seen at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. What angle does the line of sight make with the cliff face (vertical)?
example.solution: Depression is from the horizontal, so the line of sight is $30^\circ$ below horizontal; the vertical cliff makes $90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ$ with the line of sight.

tricks.title: Depression at the top equals elevation at the bottom
tricks.body:
Alternate interior angles: the depression from the observer equals the elevation measured at the object from
ground level directly below — use whichever is stated.

example.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground is $45^\circ$. What is the angle of depression of the point from the tower top?

mistakes: Measuring height from the ground instead of eye level when the observer is on a cliff, tower or building.
Using $\sin\theta$ or $\cos\theta$ where the horizontal distance makes $\tan\theta$ the right ratio.
Swapping elevation and depression (drawing the angle from the object instead of the horizontal at the eye).
subtopics.notes:
### The picture is half the answer
Every heights-and-distances question is one right triangle wearing a story. The observer's **eye** is the starting point; through it runs a dashed **horizontal line**.
- Object **above** eye level: the angle from the horizontal **up** to the line of sight is the **angle of elevation**.
- Object **below** eye level: the angle **down** from the horizontal is the **angle of depression**.

The right angle sits between the horizontal and the vertical, so the trigonometry is always $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{height above or below eye level}}{\text{horizontal distance}}$.

### Eye level, not ground level
When the observer stands on a cliff, tower or building, the height asked is measured from the **eye**, and the ground distance runs from the **base of the object**. A 1.6 m tall person watching a kite: the kite's height above ground is $1.6 + d\tan\theta$. Exams keep the observer's height either zero or clearly stated — but the *eye* is always where the horizontal starts.

### Depression mirrors elevation
The angle of depression from the observer equals the angle of elevation from the object — alternate interior angles between two parallels (the two horizontals). So "from a lighthouse the depression of a boat is $30^\circ$" converts instantly to "from the boat the elevation of the lighthouse top is $30^\circ$", and the standard-angle rules apply unchanged. This one flip solves every lighthouse, cliff and aeroplane question.

### Reading the question into the figure
Four phrases carry all the information:
- "subtends an angle $\theta$ at a point" → the elevation at that point is $\theta$;
- "the angle changes from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ as he walks $d$ **towards**" → two positions on the same side, distance $d$ apart, $\beta > \alpha$;
- "observed from the top ... the angles of depression of two ships are ..." → same-side two-angle case, gap $= h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$;
- "shadow is $k$ times the height" → $\tan(\text{sun elevation}) = \frac{1}{k}$.

### Distances that are NOT on the same line
Two points not collinear with the base (e.g. two corners of a street seen from a window): each gets its own right triangle, and the two base distances may themselves form a right angle — Pythagoras joins the party. "The bearings of the two cars differ by $90^\circ$" means their base distances are perpendicular legs and the distance between the cars is the hypotenuse. Sketch the plan view separately from the side view; exam questions love mixing the two.

### Quick revision
- Eye = origin; horizontal = baseline; elevation up, depression down.
- $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{height above/below eye level}}{\text{horizontal distance}}$.
- Depression at the top = elevation at the bottom (alternate angles).
- Observer on a platform: add the platform height at the end.
- "Subtends an angle at P" = elevation measured at P.

patterns.name: Single angle, eye-level work
patterns.howToSpot: One angle and one of {height, distance} given; the other asked — including platform/cliff eye heights.
patterns.formula: $\tan\theta = \frac{h}{d}$ w.r.t. the EYE level; add the observer's platform height if the question wants ground height.
patterns.logic:
1. Draw the horizontal through the eye; mark the angle.
2. Write one tangent equation in the unknown.
3. Add the eye height (if any) before answering ground heights.

Why: everything else in the figure is decoration — one right triangle decides.

patterns.name: Angle of depression conversions
patterns.howToSpot: Lighthouse/cliff/aeroplane looking down at boats, cars or road junctions; depression angle stated.
patterns.formula: Depression at the eye = elevation at the object; then $d = \frac{h}{\tan\theta}$. Two objects on one side → subtract the two horizontal distances.
patterns.logic:
1. Flip the depression into an elevation at the object.
2. Apply the standard-angle rule or a single tangent.
3. For two objects, compute both distances from the base and subtract.

Why: the flip turns a "looking down" story into the ordinary up-the-tower triangle.

patterns.name: Hypotenuse (thread/ladder/line-of-sight) given
patterns.howToSpot: The slant distance — thread, ladder, wire, 'direct distance' — is given instead of the horizontal.
patterns.formula: $h = L\sin\theta$, $d = L\cos\theta$: the slant line is the hypotenuse, so sine and cosine (not tangent).
patterns.logic:
1. Name the hypotenuse explicitly.
2. Height = L·sin(angle), ground distance = L·cos(angle).
3. Standard-angle values keep answers exact.

Why: tangent mixes the two legs; with the hypotenuse given, tan is the wrong tool.

patterns.name: Shadow geometry
patterns.howToSpot: A pole/building casts a shadow; the sun's elevation, the shadow length or the height is the unknown.
patterns.formula: Shadow = horizontal distance: $\tan(\text{elevation}) = \frac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$. Equal shadows at the same moment ⇒ equal heights; shadow $= \sqrt3 h$ means $30^\circ$, shadow $= h$ means $45^\circ$.
patterns.logic:
1. Sun rays make the elevation angle with the ground; the triangle is pole–shadow–ray.
2. Match the shadow:height ratio to a standard angle.
3. Two poles at the same moment share the same sun angle — set up ratios, not two triangles.

Why: the sun's angle is the same for every object at one moment, which is the entire content of "at the same time".

subtopics.title: Standard angles: 30°, 45°, 60°
subtopics.concept:
Almost every CGL question uses only these three angles. Convert tan to a **height–distance rule** and the
answer is a one-liner:

| $\theta$ | $\tan\theta$ | rule ($h$ = height, $d$ = distance) |
|---|---|---|
| $45^\circ$ | $1$ | $d=h$ |
| $30^\circ$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $d=\sqrt3\,h$ |
| $60^\circ$ | $\sqrt3$ | $d=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ |

So height from distance: $45^\circ\to h=d$; $30^\circ\to h=\frac{d}{\sqrt3}$; $60^\circ\to h=\sqrt3\,d$.
Take $\sqrt3\approx1.732$, $\sqrt2\approx1.414$ only if options are decimal.

tricks.title: Match the angle to the multiplier
tricks.body:
45° → same; 30° → distance is $\sqrt3$ times the height; 60° → height is $\sqrt3$ times the distance.
Write the multiplier before touching numbers.

example.q: A tower subtends $60^\circ$ at a point 20 m from its base. Find its height.

tricks.title: Ladder questions are sine/cosine, not tangent
tricks.body:
The ladder itself is the hypotenuse: height $=L\sin\theta$, foot distance $=L\cos\theta$. A $45^\circ$ ladder
of length $L\sqrt2$ climbs exactly $L$.

example.q: A ladder of length $10\sqrt2$ m leans at $45^\circ$. How high up the wall does it reach?

mistakes: Using the $60^\circ$ rule for $30^\circ$ (they are reciprocals: $d=\sqrt3h$ vs $d=h/\sqrt3$).
Approximating $\sqrt3$ too early and landing between two options — keep the radical until the end.
Ladder: applying $\tan\theta=h/d$ with the ladder length mistaken for $d$.
subtopics.notes:
### The three multipliers
Almost every exam question uses only $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ or $60^\circ$. Convert each to a **height–distance rule** and the tangent table becomes a cheat sheet:

| $\theta$ | $\tan\theta$ | rule ($h$ up, $d$ across) |
|---|---|---|
| $30^\circ$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $d = \sqrt3\,h$ |
| $45^\circ$ | $1$ | $d = h$ |
| $60^\circ$ | $\sqrt3$ | $d = \frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ |

Read the pair as a swap: at $30^\circ$ the distance is $\sqrt3$ times the height; at $60^\circ$ the height is $\sqrt3$ times the distance. Ratios like $\frac{h}{d}$ identify the angle from either side.

### Keeping surds exact
$\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$ and $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$ — but only reach for decimals if the options are decimal. An answer of $\frac{40}{\sqrt3}$ rationalises to $\frac{40\sqrt3}{3}$; the options may present either form, so carry the radical and match at the end. Every "odd" distractor is a surd in the wrong slot ($h\sqrt3$ vs $\frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ is the single most common trap).

### Angles that are not 30-45-60
Elevations like $15^\circ$, $75^\circ$ or $22.5^\circ$ do appear — as *differences* of standard angles. $15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ$, $75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ$; the compound expressions $\tan(45^\circ \pm \theta) = \frac{1 \pm \tan\theta}{1 \mp \tan\theta}$ finish them in one line. A question using $75^\circ$ is almost always a $45+30$ identity question in disguise.

### The ladder and the hypotenuse rule
When the slant length (ladder, thread, wire) is the given, switch to sine and cosine: $h = L\sin\theta$, $d = L\cos\theta$. The classic check: a $45^\circ$ ladder of length $L\sqrt2$ climbs exactly $L$ — the $45^\circ$ isosceles right triangle always has hypotenuse $\sqrt2$ times a leg.

### Combination moves with the same angle twice
Two objects at the same standard angle from two positions of known separation (e.g. two towers seen from a point between them at $30^°$ each, separation $D$): the heights are $\frac{D}{2\sqrt3}$ each — equal heights, equal angles. When the angles differ, each height uses its own tangent against the half-separation. A chain of two standard-angle steps (walk 10 m at 30°, then 10 m more at 45°) is just two single-angle equations written in sequence and subtracted; nothing new is needed beyond bookkeeping.

### Quick revision
- $30^\circ$: $d = \sqrt3 h$; $45^\circ$: $d = h$; $60^\circ$: $h = \sqrt3 d$.
- $\frac{h}{d} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ → 30°, $= 1$ → 45°, $= \sqrt3$ → 60°.
- Shadow $= \sqrt3 h$ at 30°; shadow $= h$ at 45°; shadow $= \frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ at 60°.
- Hypotenuse given: $L\sin\theta$ up, $L\cos\theta$ across.
- $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ are $45 \mp 30$ identities in disguise.

patterns.name: Height from distance (or reverse) at a standard angle
patterns.howToSpot: One standard angle, height or distance given, the other asked — often dressed as a tower, statue, pole or hill.
patterns.formula: $30^\circ \to d = \sqrt3 h$; $45^\circ \to d = h$; $60^\circ \to d = \frac{h}{\sqrt3}$. Keep surds exact and match the option form at the end.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the rule for the stated angle before touching numbers.
2. Substitute; rationalise only if the options demand it.
3. Check the size: 60° puts the point CLOSER than the height; 30° puts it FARTHER.

Why: the whole question is one table lookup — the difficulty is only in the surd bookkeeping.

patterns.name: Reading the angle from a ratio
patterns.howToSpot: 'The shadow is √3 times the height' or 'height equals distance' — the angle itself is the answer.
patterns.formula: $\tan\theta = \frac{h}{d}$: shadow $\sqrt3 h$ → $30^\circ$; equal → $45^\circ$; shadow $= \frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ → $60^\circ$.
patterns.logic:
1. Write tan as height over distance (shadow IS the distance).
2. Reduce the ratio to a table value.
3. Quote the angle — no further computation exists.

Why: the inverse direction of the standard rules; the same three numbers appear in reverse.

patterns.name: Ladder / wire sliding geometry
patterns.howToSpot: A ladder leaning at a standard angle; the height reached or the foot distance (or the length itself) asked.
patterns.formula: $h = L\sin\theta$, $d = L\cos\theta$. $45^\circ$ → $h = d = \frac{L}{\sqrt2}$; $30^\circ$ → $h = \frac{L}{2}$; $60^\circ$ → $h = \frac{L\sqrt3}{2}$.
patterns.logic:
1. The ladder is the hypotenuse — sin and cos only.
2. At 30° the vertical is exactly half the ladder (sin30 = ½).
3. Sanity-check with the isosceles case: 45° puts the foot at $L/\sqrt2$.

Why: 30-60-90 triangles have sides $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$ — half the ladder is the shortest side.

example.q: A ladder $20$ m long rests at $30^\circ$ against a wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

patterns.name: 45+30 identity angles (15°, 75°)
patterns.howToSpot: Elevation stated as 15° or 75°, or a tan(45°±θ) expression appears inside the question.
patterns.formula: $\tan(45^\circ \pm \theta) = \frac{1 \pm \tan\theta}{1 \mp \tan\theta}$; with $\theta = 30^\circ$: $\tan75^\circ = 2+\sqrt3$, $\tan15^\circ = 2-\sqrt3$.
patterns.logic:
1. Split the odd angle as 45 ± 30.
2. Apply the compound formula; memorise the two finished values.
3. Expect a factored surd answer $(2 \pm \sqrt3)$ — do not decimalise.

Why: 15°/75° triangles are the standard "hard" elevations; the formula turns them into one substitution.

subtopics.title: Two observation points (two angles)
subtopics.concept:
The highest-yield pattern: **two angles** from two points on the same line.

- **Same side** (walk toward the object, angle grows from $\alpha$ to $\beta$, $\beta>\alpha$):
  the distance walked equals $h(\cot\alpha-\cot\beta)$, so
  $$h=\frac{d}{\cot\alpha-\cot\beta}$$
- **Opposite sides** of the object, points $d$ apart:
  $$h=\frac{d}{\cot\alpha+\cot\beta}$$
- **From a height** (two ships seen from a lighthouse): the gap between them is
  $h(\cot\alpha-\cot\beta)$ for angles $\alpha<\beta$ measured to the nearer ship... i.e. gap $=d_{\text{far}}-d_{\text{near}}$.

With 30°/60° pairs remember $\cot30^\circ=\sqrt3$, $\cot60^\circ=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\cot30-\cot60=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$
and $h=\frac{d\sqrt3}{2}$ — the answer is $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ of the walked distance.

tricks.title: Subtract the cotangents, don't solve two triangles
tricks.body:
Write $d_1=h\cot\alpha$, $d_2=h\cot\beta$ from each position; the difference of the distances is what is
given. One linear equation in $h$.

example.q: Walking 40 m toward a tower changes the elevation angle from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the tower's height.

tricks.title: Opposite sides means add
tricks.body:
When the two observers are on opposite sides, the base distances *add up* to $d$: denominators add, not
subtract.

example.q: Two men on opposite sides of a tower 80 m apart observe its top at $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the height.

mistakes: Subtracting base distances for opposite-side observers (they add).
Using tan instead of cot in the difference formula: $d=h(\cot\alpha-\cot\beta)$, not $h(\tan\beta-\tan\alpha)$... note $\cot\alpha-\cot\beta$ with $\alpha<\beta$ is positive.
Forgetting the nearer point has the LARGER angle when assigning which distance is which.
subtopics.notes:
### The two cotangent distances
Stand $d_1$ from a tower of height $h$: the elevation is $\alpha$, so $d_1 = h\cot\alpha$. Walk closer to $d_2$: the elevation grows to $\beta$, and $d_2 = h\cot\beta$. Every two-angle question is these two equations plus one piece of information linking $d_1$ and $d_2$.

### Same side: the difference formula
Walking a distance $w$ toward the object: $w = d_1 - d_2 = h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$, so
$$h = \frac{w}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$$
The exam's favourite pair is $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$: $\cot30^\circ - \cot60^\circ = \sqrt3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, giving $h = \frac{w\sqrt3}{2}$ — the height is about $0.87$ of the walked distance. The 30–45 pair gives $h = \frac{w}{\sqrt3 - 1} = \frac{w(\sqrt3+1)}{2}$.

### Opposite sides: the sum formula
Two observers on **opposite** sides, $D$ apart: their distances **add** to $D$, so
$$h = \frac{D}{\cot\alpha + \cot\beta}$$
For the 30–60 pair: $\cot30 + \cot60 = \sqrt3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}$, so $h = \frac{D\sqrt3}{4}$. The sign inside the denominator is the whole difference between the two configurations — subtract for same side, add for opposite sides.

### Gap problems from a height
From a lighthouse $h$ high, two ships are seen at depressions $\alpha$ (far) and $\beta$ (near). Their distances from the base are $h\cot\alpha$ and $h\cot\beta$; the gap between them is
$$h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$$
— the same machinery, worked top-down. If the ships are on opposite sides, the two distances add instead.

### Two towers from a midpoint
Viewed from the midpoint of the line joining two bases, the elevations of two tower tops are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Half the separation fixes each base distance $m$; then $h_1 = m\tan\alpha$, $h_2 = m\tan\beta$, and the difference is $m(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$. Heights come from **tan** here (each tower owns its own triangle), unlike the single-tower case which is cleanest in **cot**.

### Which formula applies? (a 5-second test)
One object, two observation points: ask "are the two points on the same side of the object's base?" Same side (you walked toward it) → **difference** of cots. Opposite sides → **sum** of cots. One observer, two objects: each object gets its own cot distance from the same base point; the asked gap is their difference (same side) or sum (opposite sides). The words "walking towards", "approaching" and "on the same side" all signal subtraction; "on opposite sides", "on either side of it" signal addition.

### Quick revision
- $d = h\cot\theta$ at any observation; two observations → two equations.
- Same side (walk $w$): $h = \frac{w}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$; nearer point has the LARGER angle.
- Opposite sides (apart $D$): $h = \frac{D}{\cot\alpha + \cot\beta}$ — add, don't subtract.
- 30–60 pair: $\cot30 - \cot60 = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, $\cot30 + \cot60 = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}$.
- Gap from a height: $h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$, far minus near.
- Two towers from a midpoint: $m(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$, heights in tan.

patterns.name: Walking toward: two angles, same side
patterns.howToSpot: 'On walking x m towards the tower the elevation changes from α to β' — find the height (or the initial distance).
patterns.formula: $h = \frac{w}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$; the 30–60 pair gives $h = \frac{w\sqrt3}{2}$ instantly.
patterns.logic:
1. Write both distances as cot products of h.
2. Their difference is the walked distance — one linear equation.
3. For the distance asked instead, get h first, then $h\cot\beta$ (the near distance).

Why: subtracting two cot expressions collapses the unknown near-distance — the reason this formula exists.

patterns.name: Observers on opposite sides
patterns.howToSpot: Two people/points on opposite sides of the tower, separation given, elevations differ — height asked.
patterns.formula: $h = \frac{D}{\cot\alpha + \cot\beta}$; 30–60 pair → $h = \frac{D\sqrt3}{4}$.
patterns.logic:
1. The base distances ADD to the given separation.
2. One equation, one unknown h.
3. If the FOOT positions differ in ground level, that is a different (compound) question.

Why: "opposite sides" flips the subtraction to addition — the classic trap is reusing the same-side formula.

patterns.name: Two objects seen from a height (gap)
patterns.howToSpot: From a cliff/lighthouse, two ships/cars on the SAME side at two depressions; the gap between them asked.
patterns.formula: Gap $= h(\cot\alpha_{\text{far}} - \cot\beta_{\text{near}})$; opposite sides → $h(\cot\alpha + \cot\beta)$.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert each depression to a base distance $h\cot\theta$.
2. Same side: subtract (far − near). Opposite sides: add.
3. If the gap is given and h asked, invert the same relation.

Why: each depression independently gives a distance; the gap is just their difference on the same baseline.

example.q: From a $60$ m lighthouse the depressions of two ships on the same side are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The distance between the ships is:

patterns.name: Two towers from a midpoint / ratio of heights
patterns.howToSpot: Elevations of two tower tops from the midpoint of their bases (or a point with known base ratio); difference or ratio of heights asked.
patterns.formula: Each height = (base distance) × tan(its angle); from the midpoint, distance is the same $m$ for both: difference $= m(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the shared base distance m.
2. Height of each tower = m·tan(its elevation).
3. Difference or ratio follows; heights are 1:3 when the angles are 30° and 60°.

Why: two independent triangles share one horizontal — the midpoint makes the shared leg equal.

subtopics.title: Moving observers: speed and time
subtopics.concept:
When a car/boat/man moves between the two observation points, the distance walked is **speed × time**. Chain:

$$\text{speed}\times\text{time}=h(\cot\theta_1-\cot\theta_2)$$

then solve for $h$ (or for the speed if $h$ is given). Keep angles straight: moving **toward** the object the
angle *increases*; moving **away** it *decreases*.

tricks.title: Convert speed and time first
tricks.body: Reduce to a plain distance (e.g. $6\times6=36$ m) and the problem becomes the standard two-angle pattern.

example.q: From a tower top, a car's angle of depression changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as the car approaches at a uniform 6 m/s for 6 s. Find the tower's height.

tricks.title: Read it backwards when height is given
tricks.body:
If $h$ is known and the speed is asked, compute the gap $h(\cot\theta_1-\cot\theta_2)$ first, then divide by
time.

example.q: A car approaching a tower at a steady 4 m/s takes 5 s for the angle of elevation of the tower top to change from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the tower's height.

mistakes: Mixing units (km/h with seconds) — convert before chaining.
Assigning the larger angle to the farther position.
subtopics.notes:
### Speed and time become distance
When a car, boat or man moves between the two observation points, the walked distance is just speed × time. Chain it to the cotangent formula:
$$v \times t = h(\cot\theta_1 - \cot\theta_2)$$
and every "moving observer" question is a two-angle question in a coat. Keep units married: km/h needs hours, m/s needs seconds; $36$ km/h $= 10$ m/s is the conversion to have ready.

### The four variants
1. **Find h**: distance walked given via $v, t$; angles given → $h = \frac{vt}{\cot\theta_1 - \cot\theta_2}$.
2. **Find v or t**: h given; compute the cot-gap and divide/multiply.
3. **Depression from above**: a car approaches a tower/lighthouse; depressions *shrink* as it nears? No — as the car approaches, the depression **grows** (it looks steeper down). Moving away shrinks it. The larger angle is always the nearer position.
4. **Time to reach the base**: after the angle reaches $\beta$, the remaining distance is $h\cot\beta$; the time to the base is $\frac{h\cot\beta}{v}$.

### Direction bookkeeping
- Approaching: angle **increases** ($\theta_2 > \theta_1$), distance walked $= h(\cot\theta_1 - \cot\theta_2)$.
- Receding: angle **decreases**, walked $= h(\cot\theta_2 - \cot\theta_1)$ — same formula, angles swapped.
The identity "nearer ⇒ steeper" kills half the sign errors: if your formula gives a negative walked distance, you assigned the angles backwards.

### Boats and streamers
A boat moving toward a cliff at $u$ m/s sees the depression grow from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ in $t$ seconds: the boat covered $ut$ metres, so $ut = h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$. The distance from the cliff **after** the sighting is $h\cot\beta$; the total time to reach the cliff base is $\frac{h\cot\beta}{u}$ — a favourite "how much longer" add-on.

### Worked micro-example (every variant in one)
A $30\sqrt3$ m tower: a car's depression changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in $10$ s at constant speed. Walked: $30\sqrt3(\cot30 - \cot60) = 30\sqrt3 \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = 60$ m → speed $6$ m/s. Remaining to the base: $30\sqrt3\cot60 = 30$ m → $5$ s more. Total from first sighting: $15$ s. Reverse variants: given speed 6, find h; given h and the times, find the angles' gap; given everything, the time to the base. Same skeleton — four different questions.

### Quick revision
- $vt = h(\cot\theta_{\text{far}} - \cot\theta_{\text{near}})$: far angle is the SMALLER one.
- 30–60 pair: $vt = \frac{2h}{\sqrt3}$, so $h = \frac{vt\sqrt3}{2}$.
- After the second sighting, the remaining distance is $h\cot\theta_{\text{near}}$.
- Convert units first: km/h → m/s is ×5/18.
- Nearer ⇒ larger angle; negative answers mean swapped angles.

patterns.name: Car/boat approach: find the height
patterns.howToSpot: 'Moving at v m/s for t s the depression/elevation changes from α to β' — height of the tower/lighthouse asked.
patterns.formula: $h = \frac{vt}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$ with $\alpha$ the smaller (farther) angle; 30–60 pair → $h = \frac{vt\sqrt3}{2}$.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute the walked distance $vt$ (units consistent!).
2. Apply the same-side two-angle formula.
3. Sanity: h should be a little less than $vt\sqrt3$ for the 30–60 pair.

Why: the motion only manufactures the walked distance; the trigonometry is the standard pair.

example.q: From the top of a tower the depression of a car changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as the car approaches at $6$ m/s for $6$ s. The tower's height is:

patterns.name: Reverse: find the speed or time
patterns.howToSpot: Height given; the speed (or time) for the angle to change from α to β asked.
patterns.formula: Walked distance $= h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$; then $v = \frac{\text{distance}}{t}$ or $t = \frac{\text{distance}}{v}$.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute the cot-gap distance first.
2. Divide by the given time (for speed) or speed (for time).
3. "How much longer to reach the base" adds $\frac{h\cot\beta}{v}$.

Why: the geometry fixes the distance; rate arithmetic finishes it.

example.q: A car travelling at $4$ m/s takes $5$ s for the elevation of a tower top to rise from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The tower's height is:

patterns.name: Time to reach the foot of the object
patterns.howToSpot: After the second angle is observed, how much longer until the observer is at the base — or the total journey time.
patterns.formula: Remaining distance $= h\cot\beta$ (the near angle); time $= \frac{h\cot\beta}{v}$. Total time adds the elapsed $t$.
patterns.logic:
1. Find h from the first leg.
2. The remaining leg is the near distance $h\cot\beta$.
3. Divide by v; add elapsed time only if "total" is asked.

Why: the near cotangent distance IS what is left to travel — no new trigonometry needed.

example.q: A car at $6$ m/s watched from a $18\sqrt{3}$ m tower sees its depression grow from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. After the second sighting, the time to reach the tower base is:

patterns.name: Two moving observers / positions from motion
patterns.howToSpot: Two cars/boats approach the same tower on one road, or one object moves while a fixed position is tracked.
patterns.formula: Each observer owns a cot-distance from the base; the gap between two approaching vehicles closes at the SUM of speeds.
patterns.logic:
1. Write each position as a cot product of h where angles are known.
2. For two vehicles approaching each other, the gap closes at (u + v).
3. Solve the linear condition stated (meeting time, gap, who is where).

Why: the trigonometry pins positions; relative-speed arithmetic tracks their change — two separate layers.

example.q: Two cars approach a tower from the same road. When the slower car is $60\sqrt{3}$ m away, its elevation of the tower top is $30^\circ$. The tower's height is:
example.solution: $h = 60\sqrt3\tan30^\\circ = 60$ m (speeds matter for later time questions, not for h).

subtopics.title: Compound figures: buildings, pedestals, broken objects
subtopics.concept:
Split the figure at the **eye-level horizontal** and handle each piece with its own angle:

- **Statue on a pedestal**: pedestal gives the distance ($d=\text{pedestal}\cdot\cot45^\circ$ etc.); the statue is
  $d(\tan\beta-\tan\alpha)$ for bottom/top angles $\alpha,\beta$.
- **Tower on a building**: tower $=d\tan(\text{top})-$ building height.
- **Broken tree**: the fallen part is the hypotenuse. If the top touches ground at distance $b$ making angle
  $\theta$, broken part $=\frac{b}{\cos\theta}$, standing part $=b\tan\theta$, and the whole tree is their sum.

tricks.title: Angles differ by 15°? Expect a surd answer
tricks.body:
45° paired with 60° or 30° gives clean radicals; keep $(\sqrt3-1)$ or $(1+\sqrt3)$ factored — that exact
form is what the options show.

example.q: A statue stands on a 30 m pedestal. From a point on the ground the elevation of the pedestal top is $45^\circ$ and of the statue top $60^\circ$. Find the statue's height.

tricks.title: Broken tree = broken + standing
tricks.body:
Work the right triangle of the fallen part: horizontal $b$, angle $\theta$ at the tip. Standing part
$=b\tan\theta$, fallen part $=\frac{b}{\cos\theta}$; add them.

example.q: A tree breaks and the top touches the ground 15 m from the base, making $30^\circ$ with the ground. Find the original height.

mistakes: Forgetting the standing/building part and reporting only the extra piece.
Adding the fallen length and the standing height with the angle applied to the wrong side.
Rationalising $30(\sqrt3-1)$ into a decimal when the options are in factored surd form.
subtopics.notes:
### Split at the eye-level horizontal
Compound figures stack two objects — statue on a pedestal, tower on a building, flagstaff on a tower. One horizontal line through the **change point** (where the pedestal meets the statue, where the building ends) splits the figure into two right triangles that share a base distance $d$.

### The workhorse: difference of two tangents
From a ground point, the elevation of the pedestal top is $\alpha$ and of the statue top is $\beta$:
- Pedestal: $p = d\tan\alpha$.
- Whole: $p + s = d\tan\beta$.
- **Statue**: $s = d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$.

The $\alpha = 45^\circ$ special case is everywhere: it fixes $d = p$ (the pedestal height IS the distance), so the statue is $p(\tan\beta - 1)$.

### Tower on a building from a distance
Building $b$, tower $t$, elevation of building top $\alpha$, of tower top $\beta$ from distance $d$: $b = d\tan\alpha$, $b + t = d\tan\beta$, so $t = d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$. Same equation, different furniture. When the observation point is instead on the **roof** (elevation of the tower top $\beta$, depression of the base $\alpha$), the depression fixes the distance: $d = \frac{b}{\tan\alpha}$, and the tower is $d\tan\beta$ — don't forget to ADD the building back.

### The broken tree (and its cousins)
A tree breaks; the standing part $a$ and the broken part $L$ form a right triangle with the ground: $L$ is the hypotenuse, the distance $b$ where the top touches is one leg, $a$ the other. Given the touch distance $b$ and the ground angle $\theta$:
- standing part $a = b\tan\theta$
- broken part $L = \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$
- original height $= a + L = b\tan\theta + \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$
The original height reappears in "the tree is $H$ m tall — where does it touch?" questions: solve $\frac{b}{\cos\theta} = H - b\tan\theta$ or use the identity $L^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

### Windows: two elevations, one structure
Two windows in a building are observed from a point: elevations $\alpha$ and $\beta$ ($\beta > \alpha$), window heights differ by $k$ m. Then $k = d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$ — the same difference-of-tangents machinery, and the reverse direction (find $d$) needs only a division.

### Quick revision
- Shared base $d$: upper piece $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$.
- $45^\circ$ below ⇒ $d$ = lower piece's height.
- Broken tree: standing $b\tan\theta$, broken $\frac{b}{\cos\theta}$; add for the original.
- Roof observation: depression gives $d$; add the building height back.
- Options in factored surds $((\sqrt3-1)$, $(\sqrt3+1))$ — keep them factored.

patterns.name: Statue on a pedestal
patterns.howToSpot: Pedestal + statue observed from one point: elevation of the pedestal top and of the statue top given.
patterns.formula: Statue $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$; if $\alpha = 45^\circ$ then $d$ = pedestal height and statue $= p(\tan\beta - 1)$.
patterns.logic:
1. The lower angle fixes d (or the lower object's height).
2. Whole = d·tan(upper angle); subtract the lower piece.
3. Keep $(\sqrt3-1)$ factored if the options do.

Why: both triangles share the horizontal — one subtraction separates the statue.

example.q: A statue stands on a $30$ m pedestal. From a ground point the elevations of the pedestal top and statue top are $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The statue's height is:

patterns.name: Tower on a building (ground observer)
patterns.howToSpot: From a ground point, elevations of the building top and the tower top (on the building) both given.
patterns.formula: Building $= d\tan\alpha$; tower $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$ where $\beta$ is the top angle.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute the building height first.
2. Whole structure = d·tanβ; tower = whole − building.
3. If d itself is unknown, one of the two heights is usually given to fix it.

Why: identical algebra to the statue question — the exam just changes the furniture.

example.q: A tower stands on a building. From a point $20\sqrt{3}$ m away, the elevations of the building top and tower top are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The tower's height is:

patterns.name: Roof observation: elevation up + depression down
patterns.howToSpot: From the roof of a building: elevation of the tower top AND depression of the tower base both given.
patterns.formula: Depression $\alpha$ fixes $d = \frac{b}{\tan\alpha}$ (b = building height); tower $= b + d\tan\beta$.
patterns.logic:
1. The depression gives the horizontal: $d = b\cot\alpha$.
2. The elevation adds the part above the roof: $d\tan\beta$.
3. ADD the building height — the top angle knows nothing about it.

Why: the observer's horizontal is at roof level; the tower's base is below it. Forgetting the building is the classic trap.

example.q: From a $7$ m high building roof, the elevation of a tower top is $60^\circ$ and the depression of its base is $45^\circ$. The tower's height is:

patterns.name: Broken tree / pole
patterns.howToSpot: A tree/pole breaks and the top touches the ground at a distance, making an angle; the original height (or a part) asked.
patterns.formula: Standing $= b\tan\theta$, broken $= \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$; original $= b\tan\theta + \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$.
patterns.logic:
1. The touch distance b and ground angle θ define the triangle.
2. Standing part: opposite leg; broken part: hypotenuse.
3. Add for the original height; the broken part never "stands" again.

Why: the fallen piece is the hypotenuse — reading it as the vertical is the standard error.

example.q: A tree breaks and its top touches the ground $15$ m from the base, making $30^\circ$ with the ground. The original height of the tree was:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One angle (30°, 45° or 60°) with either the height or the distance given.
pyqPatterns.approach: Standard-angle rule: $d = h$ at 45°, $d = \sqrt3 h$ at 30°, $d = \frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ at 60°; keep the radical until the option match.

example.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 50 m tower from a point on the ground is $60^\circ$. The distance of the point from the base is:

pyqPatterns.pattern: Angle of depression from a height
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Lighthouse/cliff/aeroplane looking down at ships, cars or buildings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Depression at the eye = elevation at the object; then $d = h\cot\theta$. Two objects → subtract (same side) or add (opposite sides) the two distances.

example.q: From a 100 m cliff the depression of a boat is $30^\circ$. Its distance from the cliff base is:

pyqPatterns.pattern: Two angles from two points (walking or opposite sides)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Elevation changes from α to β after walking $w$ m, or two observers $D$ apart on opposite sides.

example.q: Walking 40 m towards a tower changes the elevation from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A car/boat moves at uniform speed; the depression or elevation changes after a stated time.
pyqPatterns.approach: Distance = speed × time $= h(\cot\theta_{\text{far}} - \cot\theta_{\text{near}})$; solve for $h$, $v$ or $t$. Remaining distance to the base is $h\cot\theta_{\text{near}}$.

example.q: At 6 m/s a car's depression changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in 6 s. The tower's height is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A statue on a pedestal, tower on a building, or flagstaff on a tower; two elevations from one point.
pyqPatterns.approach: Split at the change point: upper piece $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$; a 45° lower angle fixes $d$ = lower height. Roof observations: add the building back.

example.q: A statue on a 30 m pedestal is seen at $45^\circ$ (pedestal top) and $60^\circ$ (statue top). The statue's height is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Shadow length related to height (equal, √3 times, or a ratio), possibly two objects at once.
pyqPatterns.approach: Shadow = horizontal distance: $\tan(\text{elevation}) = \frac{h}{\text{shadow}}$. Equal shadows ⇒ equal heights; two objects at one moment share the sun's angle — use ratios.

example.q: A stick 1.5 m casts a 2.5 m shadow while a tower casts 75 m. The tower's height is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A tree breaks and the top touches the ground at a stated distance and ground angle.
pyqPatterns.approach: Standing $= b\tan\theta$; broken (hypotenuse) $= \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$; original height $= b\tan\theta + \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$.

example.q: A tree breaks; the top touches ground 15 m away at $30^\circ$. The original height is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The slant distance is given with the angle; a height or ground distance asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: $h = L\sin\theta$, $d = L\cos\theta$ — sine/cosine, never tangent, when the hypotenuse is the given.

example.q: A 60 m cable makes $60^\circ$ with the ground. The pole height is:

solvedExamples.shortcut: At $45^\circ$, distance = height — no calculation at all. (Diagram: eye at the point, horizontal to the tower, angle up to the top.)

solvedExamples.q: The shadow of a tower is $40\sqrt{3}$ m long when the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 30° → height = $\frac{\text{shadow}}{\sqrt3}=\frac{40\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=40$ m. The $\sqrt3$ cancels by design.

solvedExamples.q: From the top of a 100 m high cliff, the angle of depression of a ship is $30^\circ$. Find the distance of the ship from the base of the cliff.
solvedExamples.solution:
Depression $30^\circ$ = elevation $30^\circ$ at the ship. $\tan30^\circ=\frac{100}{d}$

$\frac{1}{\sqrt3}=\frac{100}{d}\Rightarrow d=100\sqrt3$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Flip depression to elevation, then the 30° rule: $d=\sqrt3\times100=100\sqrt3$ m. Trap: $\frac{100}{\sqrt3}$ (that is the 60° answer).

solvedExamples.q: Walking 40 m towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.
solvedExamples.solution:
Let $h$ be the height and $x$ the nearer distance. Then $x\tan60^\circ=h$ and $(x+40)\tan30^\circ=h$:

$h\cot60^\circ+40=h\cot30^\circ\Rightarrow40=h(\sqrt3-\frac{1}{\sqrt3})=\frac{2h}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow h=20\sqrt3$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Direct formula: $h=\frac{d}{\cot30-\cot60}=\frac{40\sqrt3}{2}=20\sqrt3$ m. For a 30–60 pair the height is always $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ of the walked distance.

solvedExamples.q: A statue stands on a 30 m high pedestal. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of the top of the pedestal is $45^\circ$ and that of the top of the statue is $60^\circ$. Find the height of the statue.
solvedExamples.solution:
From the $45^\circ$ observation: $d=\frac{30}{\tan45^\circ}=30$ m.

From the $60^\circ$ observation: $30+\text{statue}=30\tan60^\circ=30\sqrt3$.

So statue $=30\sqrt3-30=30(\sqrt3-1)$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 45° fixes $d$ = pedestal height; statue $=d(\tan60-\tan45)=30(\sqrt3-1)$. Keep the factored surd — that is how the options read.

practice.q: A vertical pole 12 m high casts a shadow on level ground when the sun's elevation is $45^\circ$. The length of the shadow is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → shadow = height = 12 m.

practice.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 30 m high tower from a point on the ground is $60^\circ$. The distance of the point from the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → distance $=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m. Trap: $30\sqrt3$ (that is the 30° rule).

practice.q: From the top of a 60 m high lighthouse, the angle of depression of a boat is $60^\circ$. The horizontal distance of the boat from the lighthouse is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → $d=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}=20\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: If the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$ and a tower's shadow is $30\sqrt{3}$ m long, the height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30° → height = shadow ÷ $\sqrt3$ = 30 m.

practice.q: A ladder 20 m long leans against a wall at $45^\circ$ to the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
practice.shortcut: Ladder is the hypotenuse: $h=L\sin\theta$. At 45°: $h=\frac{L}{\sqrt2}$. Trap: 10 is the $\frac{L}{2}$ guess.

practice.q: Two men stand on opposite sides of a tower, 80 m apart, and observe its top at elevations of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Opposite sides → add the cotangents: $\frac{80}{\frac{4}{\sqrt3}}=20\sqrt3$ m. Trap: subtracting gives $\frac{80\sqrt3}{2}=40\sqrt3$ (wrong side of the figure).

practice.q: On walking 20 m towards a tower the angle of elevation of its top rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30–60 pair: $h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times d=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times20=10\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: The shadow of a pole is $\sqrt{3}$ times the height of the pole. The angle of elevation of the sun is:
practice.shortcut: Shadow $\sqrt3\times$ height is the signature of 30° ($d=\sqrt3h$). Trap: 60° inverts the ratio.

practice.q: From the top of a 60 m high lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships on the same side are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The distance between the ships is:
practice.solution:
Distances from the base: far $=60\cot30^\circ=60\sqrt3$, near $=60\cot60^\circ=\frac{60}{\sqrt3}=20\sqrt3$.

Gap $=60\sqrt3-20\sqrt3=40\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Gap $=h(\cot30-\cot60)=60\cdot\frac2{\sqrt3}=40\sqrt3$ m — same $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times$ nothing; here $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3}$. Watch: far minus near, never add.

practice.q: From a point 20$\sqrt{3}$ m from the base of a building, the elevation of the top of the building is $30^\circ$ and of the top of the tower standing on it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution:
Building: $h_b=20\sqrt3\tan30^\circ=20$ m.

Building + tower: $20\sqrt3\tan60^\circ=60$ m. Tower $=60-20=40$ m.
practice.shortcut: $\text{tower}=d(\tan60-\tan30)=20\sqrt3(\sqrt3-\frac1{\sqrt3})=20\sqrt3\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt3}=40$ m.

practice.q: A tree breaks due to a storm and the broken part touches the ground 15 m from the base, making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the tree before breaking was:
practice.solution:
Fallen part $=\frac{15}{\cos30^\circ}=\frac{30}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m; standing part $=15\tan30^\circ=5\sqrt3$ m.

Total $=15\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Tree $=\frac{b}{\cos\theta}+b\tan\theta=10\sqrt3+5\sqrt3=15\sqrt3$. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ (forgotten standing part).

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the tops of two towers from the midpoint of the line joining their bases are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. If the towers are 60 m apart, the difference of their heights is:
practice.solution:
Each base is 30 m from the midpoint.

$h_1=30\tan30^\circ=10\sqrt3$, $h_2=30\tan60^\circ=30\sqrt3$. Difference $=20\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Midpoint splits 60 into 30 + 30; heights are $30\times\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $30\times\sqrt3$ → difference $20\sqrt3$ m. (Ratio check: heights are always 1 : 3 here.)

practice.q: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ while the car approaches uniformly at 6 m/s for 6 seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Speed × time gives the walked distance; then the 30–60 pair: $h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times36=18\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points 40 m apart on the same side of it are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{40}{\sqrt3-1}$ → multiply by $\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3+1}$ → $20(\sqrt3+1)$ m. The $30/45$ pair always ends in $(\sqrt3+1)\times\frac{d}{2}$.

practice.q: From the roof of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $60^\circ$ and the angle of depression of its base is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution:
Depression $45^\circ$: horizontal distance $d=\frac{7}{\tan45^\circ}=7$ m.

Elevation $60^\circ$: top above roof $=7\tan60^\circ=7\sqrt3$.

Tower $=7+7\sqrt3=7(1+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: 45° depression gives $d$ = building height (7); tower $=7+7\sqrt3$. Add the building back — the top angle only measures the part above the roof.

practice.q: A kite is flying with $30^\circ$ elevation from a point on level ground. If the kite's thread (assumed straight) is $100$ m long, the kite's height above the ground is:
practice.shortcut: Hypotenuse × sin. Trap: $50\sqrt3$ — that uses cos.

practice.q: From a $20$ m high tower, the angle of depression of a car on level ground is $45^\circ$. The car's distance from the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → distance = height. Trap: $20\sqrt3$ — that is the 30° rule.

practice.q: A cable of length $60$ m runs from the top of a pole to the ground, making $60^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the pole is:
practice.shortcut: Hypotenuse × sin60. Trap: $60\sqrt3$ — forgetting to halve.

practice.q: A vertical stick $1.5$ m long casts a shadow $2.5$ m long. At the same time, a nearby tower casts a shadow $75$ m long. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Ratio trick: height = shadow × (stick/shadow-stick) = $75 × 0.6$.

practice.q: A ladder of length $30$ m leans against a wall at $60^\circ$ to the ground. The foot of the ladder is at what distance from the wall?
practice.shortcut: Cos for the ground leg. Trap: $15\sqrt3$ — that is the wall height side.

practice.q: From the top of a cliff $80$ m high, the angle of depression of a ship is $45^\circ$. The distance of the ship from the foot of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: 45° flip → distance = height.

practice.q: A straight wire from the top of a $50$ m tower reaches the ground $50$ m from the base. The angle the wire makes with the ground is:
practice.solution: $\tan\theta = \frac{50}{50} = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ$ (the wire length $50\sqrt2$ m is a distractor).
practice.shortcut: Height = ground distance → 45°. Trap: using the wire as if tangent asked for it.

practice.q: The shadow of a tower is $18$ m long when the sun's elevation is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → shadow = height.

practice.q: From a point on the ground, the elevation of an aeroplane is $60^\circ$. If the plane is $1000$ m away along the line of sight, its height above the ground is:
practice.shortcut: Line of sight = hypotenuse: sin60. Trap: $1000\sqrt3$ (used tan60 on the hypotenuse).

practice.q: A pole $10$ m high casts a shadow $25$ m long. At the same moment, the shadow of a building is $90$ m. The building's height is:
practice.shortcut: $90 × \frac{10}{25} = 36$. Trap: $40$ — dividing 90 by the pole height ratio inverted.

practice.q: From a $\frac{80}{\sqrt{3}}$ m high tower, the angles of depression of two cars due north of it are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The distance between the cars is:
practice.shortcut: Far minus near, both scaled by $h$. Trap: $\frac{160\sqrt3}{3}$ — a slipped surd.

practice.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point $30\sqrt{3}$ m from its base is $30^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30° → distance is √3 × height; divide back.

practice.q: A tree casts a shadow $60$ m long when the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$. The height of the tree is:
practice.shortcut: 30°: height = shadow/√3 = $60/\sqrt3 = 20\sqrt3$. Trap: 20 — dividing twice.

practice.q: A pole casts a shadow equal to its own height. The sun's angle of elevation is:
practice.shortcut: Equal shadow and height is the 45° signature.

practice.q: From a point $15$ m from the base of a flagstaff, the elevation of its top is $60^\circ$. The height of the flagstaff is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → height = √3 × distance. Trap: $5\sqrt3$ — that is the distance rule inverted.

practice.q: A ladder $20$ m long rests against a wall at $30^\circ$ to the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
practice.shortcut: sin30 = ½ → half the ladder. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ — that is the foot distance ($20\cos30$).

practice.q: The elevation of a hilltop from a point $45$ m away (horizontal) is $60^\circ$. The hill's height is:
practice.shortcut: 60° multiplies the distance by √3.

practice.q: The value of $\tan^2 75^\circ + \tan^2 15^\circ$ is:
A $12$ m ladder leans at $45^\circ$ against a vertical wall. The height it reaches is:
practice.shortcut: 45°: height = $\frac{L}{\sqrt2} = 6\sqrt2$. Trap: 6 — that would be sin30.

practice.q: A tower subtends $75^\circ$ at a point $10$ m from its base (horizontal). Its height is:
practice.shortcut: $\tan75^\circ = 2+\sqrt3$ from the 45+30 identity. Keep it factored.

practice.q: The shadow of a tower is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ times its height. The sun's elevation is:
practice.shortcut: Short shadow means a HIGH sun: 60°. Trap: 30° — the reciprocal ratio.

practice.q: On walking $40$ m towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30–60 pair: $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} × 40$. Trap: $40\sqrt3$ — forgot the ½ factor.

practice.q: Two men stand on opposite sides of a tower, $40$ m apart. They observe the top at elevations $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Opposite sides add: $\frac{D\sqrt3}{4}$. Trap: $20\sqrt3$ — same-side formula (subtracted).

practice.q: From the top of a $60$ m lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships due east of it are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The distance between the ships is:
practice.shortcut: Gap $= h · \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = 40\sqrt3$. Trap: adding the distances.

practice.q: The elevations of the tops of two towers from the midpoint of the line joining their bases are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. If the towers are $60$ m apart, the difference of their heights is:
practice.shortcut: Heights at 30°/60° from equal bases are 1:3 → difference is $2 × 10\sqrt3$.

practice.q: Two poles of equal height stand at the two ends of a $30$ m segment. From the midpoint of the segment, the elevation of each top is $60^\circ$. The height of each pole is:
practice.solution: Midpoint is $15$ m from each base: $h = 15\tan60^\\circ = 15\\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Equal angles at the midpoint ⇒ equal heights; one tangent finishes it. Trap: $15$ — dropping the multiplier.

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points $20$ m apart on the same side are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Rationalise $\frac{20}{\sqrt3-1}$ by multiplying $(\sqrt3+1)/(\sqrt3+1)$.

practice.q: Two men on opposite sides of a $50\sqrt{3}$ m high tower are $100$ m apart. The smaller of the two elevation angles of the top is:
practice.solution: $\cot\alpha + \cot\beta = \frac{100}{50\sqrt3} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$. The 30–60 pair sums to $\frac{4}{\sqrt3}$ — too big; 45–60: $1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3} \approx 1.577 > 1.155$. Try 60–60: $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ exactly. So both are $60^\circ$; the smaller is $60^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{D}{h} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = \cot60 + \cot60$ — symmetric case: both angles 60°.

practice.q: From a cliff, the depressions of two boats on the same side at distances $15\sqrt{3}$ m apart are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 15\sqrt3 \Rightarrow h = 22.5$ m. (Trust the algebra over pretty options.)

practice.q: Walking $50(\sqrt{3}-1)$ m towards a hill changes its elevation from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. The height of the hill is:
practice.shortcut: The walk distance was engineered to cancel the denominator.

practice.q: Two observers on opposite sides of a tower are $40(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ m apart and see its top at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: $h = \frac{40(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3})}{1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}} = 40$ m... careful: $\cot45^\circ = 1$, $\cot60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, sum $= 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ exactly, so $h = 40$ m.
practice.shortcut: The separation equals h × (sum of cots) — here the sum is exactly the given factor.

practice.q: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ while the car approaches uniformly at $6$ m/s for $6$ seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{vt\sqrt3}{2} = 18\sqrt3$. Trap: 36 — treating the walk as the height.

practice.q: A boat approaching a cliff at $5$ m/s sees the angle of depression of its top change from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ in $4$ seconds. The height of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: Rationalise: $\frac{20(\sqrt3+1)}{2}$.

practice.q: A car moving at $4$ m/s takes $5$ seconds for the elevation of a tower's top to change from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{vt\sqrt3}{2}$ again — the 30–60 pair is worth memorising.

practice.q: From an $18\sqrt{3}$ m high tower, a car's depression grows from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as it approaches at $6$ m/s. The time (in seconds) it now takes to reach the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Near distance $h\cot60$ over speed. Trap: $3\sqrt3$ — using the FAR distance.

practice.q: The elevation of a $10$ m pole's top changes from $45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as a cyclist approaches. The distance cycled is:
practice.shortcut: Far $h\cot45 = 10$, near $\frac{10}{\sqrt3}$; difference $10 - \frac{10}{\sqrt3}$.

practice.q: A man walking at $2$ m/s towards a tower finds the elevation changing from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in $9$ seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{18\sqrt3}{2} = 9\sqrt3$.

practice.q: A tower is $15\sqrt{3}$ m high. A car's depression angle from the top grows from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as the car approaches at $5$ m/s. The time for this change is:
practice.shortcut: Cot-gap distance ÷ speed. Trap: 2 s — halving instead of multiplying.

practice.q: Walking $3\sqrt{3}$ m towards a pole raises the elevation of its top from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The pole's height is:
practice.solution: $h = \frac{3\sqrt3 \cdot \sqrt3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}$ m... exact: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 3\sqrt3 \Rightarrow h = \frac{9}{2} = 4.5$ m. With the closest clean option set, $h = 3\sqrt3/1.5$... recompute cleanly: $h = \frac{3\sqrt3 \times \sqrt3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}$ m.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = vt$ with $vt = 3\sqrt3$ gives $h = \frac{9}{2}$ m — trust the algebra.

practice.q: From a tower of height $15$ m, a cyclist's depression grows from $45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as he rides at $3$ m/s. After the second sighting, the time to reach the tower base is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{h\cot60}{v} = \frac{5\sqrt3}{3}$ s. (Keep the surd exact.)

practice.q: A cyclist rides toward a $12\sqrt{3}$ m pole at $6$ m/s; the elevation of the pole top rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The cycling time for this change is:
practice.solution: Gap $= 12\sqrt3\cot30^\circ - 12\sqrt3\cot60^\circ = 36 - 12 = 24$ m; time $= \frac{24}{6} = 4$ s... exact: $\frac{24}{6} = 4$ s.
practice.shortcut: Cot-gap ÷ speed. Trap: 2 s — halving the gap.

practice.q: A boat moving at $4$ m/s holds a straight course toward a cliff; the elevation of its top rises from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ over $10(\sqrt{3}+1)$ seconds. The cliff's height is:
practice.solution: Sailed: $4 \times 10(\sqrt3+1) = 40(\sqrt3+1)$ m $= h(\cot30\circ - \cot45\circ) = h(\sqrt3-1)$, so $h = \frac{40(\sqrt3+1)^2}{2} = 20(4+2\sqrt3) = 40(2+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: Rationalise by $(\sqrt3+1)$: the square gives $4+2\sqrt3$; factor out 2. Trap: $20(\sqrt3+1)$ — dropping the square.

practice.q: A train moving at $20$ m/s passes a signal post; the depression of a point on the track $2$ s later is $45^\circ$ from a $50$ m high signal bridge. How far is the train from the bridge base $2$ s after passing the post?
practice.solution: Covered $20 \times 2 = 40$ m; remaining to the bridge base $= 50\cot45^\circ = 50$ m.
practice.shortcut: Motion gives the distance; the cot gives what remains. Trap: 90 — adding instead of tracking remaining.

practice.q: A statue stands on a $30$ m high pedestal. From a point on the ground, the elevation of the top of the pedestal is $45^\circ$ and that of the top of the statue is $60^\circ$. The height of the statue is:
practice.shortcut: 45° fixes d = pedestal height. Trap: $30\sqrt3$ — that is the whole structure.

practice.q: From a point $20\sqrt{3}$ m from the base of a building, the elevation of the top of the building is $30^\circ$ and of the top of the tower standing on it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: Building $= 20\sqrt3\tan30^\circ = 20$ m; whole $= 20\sqrt3\tan60^\circ = 60$ m; tower $= 40$ m.

practice.q: From the roof of a $7$ m high building, the elevation of the top of a tower is $60^\circ$ and the depression of its base is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: Depression 45°: $d = 7$ m. Above-roof part $= 7\tan60^\circ = 7\sqrt3$. Tower $= 7 + 7\sqrt3 = 7(1+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: Add the building back — the top angle only sees the part above the roof.

practice.q: A tree breaks due to a storm; the top touches the ground $15$ m from the base, making $30^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the tree before breaking was:
practice.shortcut: $b\tan\theta + \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ — forgot the standing part.

practice.q: A flagstaff stands on a $10$ m high tower. From a point on the ground, the elevation of the tower top is $45^\circ$ and of the flagstaff top is $60^\circ$. The flagstaff's length is:
practice.shortcut: 45° below ⇒ d = 10; upper piece $= d(\tan60 - \tan45)$.

practice.q: The elevations of the bottom and the top of a $20$ m tall antenna on a building, from a point on the ground, are $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the building is:
practice.shortcut: Antenna $= d(\sqrt3 - 1)$; building $= d$; solve d from the antenna first. Trap: $10(\sqrt3+1)$ — that is the BUILDING.

practice.q: A $15\sqrt{3}$ m high pole breaks and the top touches the ground making $30^\circ$ with the ground. At what distance from the base does the top touch the ground?
practice.solution: Standing $= b\tan30^\circ = \frac{b}{\sqrt3}$; broken $= \frac{b}{\cos30^\circ} = \frac{2b}{\sqrt3}$. Sum $= \frac{3b}{\sqrt3} = b\sqrt3 = 15\sqrt3 \Rightarrow b = 15$ m.
practice.shortcut: $b\tan30 + \frac{b}{\cos30} = b\sqrt3$ when θ = 30° — solve for b.

practice.q: From the top of a cliff, the depressions of the top and the foot of a $9$ m tall lighthouse are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the cliff is:
practice.solution: Let cliff $= H$, horizontal $= d$: $H - 9 = d\tan30^\circ$ and $H = d\tan60^\circ$. Subtract: $9 = d(\sqrt3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt3}) = \frac{2d}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow d = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}$; $H = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\sqrt3 = 13.5$ m.
practice.shortcut: Two cot equations, subtract the lighthouse. Trap: $9\sqrt3$ — that is $H - 9$'s neighbour, not H.

practice.q: A bamboo $\sqrt{13}$ m high breaks; the top touches the ground $2$ m from the stem. The height of the break above the ground is:
practice.solution: Standing $a$, broken $\sqrt{13 - a^2} = 2$ (hypotenuse check: $a^2 + 2^2 = 13$) $\Rightarrow a^2 = 9 \Rightarrow a = 3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Pythagoras: standing$^2$ + touch distance$^2$ = original$^2$.
